title: Who Owns a Name
bigQuestion: When two groups claim the same martial art name, which records can settle who holds it, and which records cannot?

story.title: Three Letters on a Door
story.kicker: A lawyer and a teacher read the same sign on a school door in two different ways.
paragraphs: A small taekwondo school sits between a bakery and a tax office. Painted on its glass door are three letters: ITF. Below them is the teacher's name and a phone number. One evening a lawyer stops by. She is helping a client open a new school across town, and her client wants to use the same three letters.

The teacher points to a framed certificate on the wall. It is signed by an officer of the International Taekwon-Do Federation. "These letters belong to the federation that promoted me," he says. The lawyer nods, then explains a problem. Since 2002, several different groups have each called themselves the International Taekwon-Do Federation. Each one issues its own certificates.

"So which group owns the letters?" the teacher asks. The lawyer says it depends on the question. A trademark office keeps one kind of record. A federation keeps another kind in its rank register. A founder's writings, a court ruling and a newspaper story are each a different kind of evidence.

They sit down at the front desk. The teacher opens a binder of old tournament programs. The lawyer opens a laptop to a public trademark search. For the next hour, they do not argue about who is the better teacher. They argue about which papers answer which question.
story.think: The teacher and the lawyer look at different records. What question can each kind of record answer?

lessons.title: Scrolls in the Old Schools
lessons.mainIdea: In early modern Japan, a martial school's head controlled its name by granting written licenses, such as the menkyo kaiden.
reading: In Japan before 1868, many martial traditions were organized as a *ryū*, a school with its own name, founder story and line of heads. A ryū might teach swordsmanship, archery or unarmed arts. Membership was often tied to a domain or a family. The school's name was a kind of property that its head protected.

A ryū marked a student's progress with written scrolls called licenses. The highest was often the *menkyo kaiden*, meaning "license of complete transmission." It stated that the holder had received the full teaching of that school. A person holding it could often teach and pass the school's name on.

A related pattern, the *iemoto* system, grew in Edo-period (1603–1868) arts such as the tea ceremony and flower arranging. In it, one head of a family line holds final authority over licenses. Historians note that license fees could help support a school's head. The same idea of a chain of permission shaped several martial schools.

words.d: a named Japanese school or tradition with its own line of heads
"license of complete transmission"; the top written license in many old Japanese schools
a system in which one family head holds final authority over a school's licenses
a line of teachers and students through which a school's name passes

check.why: The reading names the tea ceremony and flower arranging as Edo-period arts organized by the iemoto system.

lessons.title: Kanō's Numbered Ranks
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō Jigorō's Kodokan replaced scroll licenses with numbered dan grades recorded in its own register, a model many arts later copied.
reading: In 1882, Kanō Jigorō opened the *Kodokan* in a room at Eishō-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. He had studied older jujutsu schools. He wanted a school that fit a modern country with public schools and written rules. The Kodokan kept careful records of every student who joined.

In 1883, Kanō gave the first *dan* grades to two students, Saigō Shirō and Tomita Tsunejirō. A dan is a numbered grade, counted upward from first dan. Unlike a scroll written for one student, a numbered rank could be compared across hundreds of students. The Kodokan kept each promotion in its register.

Colored belts for beginners came later. Kawaishi Mikinosuke, a Japanese teacher who moved to France in the 1930s, is widely credited with spreading a system of many colors for the grades below dan, called *kyū*. Today a Kodokan certificate is still a record that anyone can ask the Kodokan to confirm.

words.d: the judo school and headquarters Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882
a numbered rank counted upward from first dan
a grade below the dan ranks, often shown by colored belts

check.q: What made a numbered dan rank different from an old scroll license?

check.why: Numbered dan ranks could be compared across many students, and the Kodokan recorded each one.

check.q: Who is widely credited with spreading many-colored kyū belts in France?
check.why: Kawaishi Mikinosuke, who moved to France in the 1930s, is widely credited with the many-color kyū system.

lessons.title: A Registry in Seoul
lessons.mainIdea: The Kukkiwon in Seoul, founded in 1972, issues taekwondo dan and poom certificates to students in many countries and keeps them in one registry.
reading: The *Kukkiwon* is a large hall in the Gangnam district of Seoul. Its building was finished in November 1972. The Korean government backed it as a central home for taekwondo. The name is often translated as "national gymnasium" or "national technique hall."

The Kukkiwon issues rank certificates for taekwondo. Adults receive dan ranks. Students under fifteen receive *poom* ranks, a junior form of black-belt rank that can be changed to dan later. A school anywhere in the world can apply to register its students. Each certificate carries a number that can be checked in the Kukkiwon's records.

A central registry changes how a teacher proves a claim. A school's owner may say he trained in Korea. A Kukkiwon number is a record another person can look up. Many national taekwondo bodies and the World Taekwondo federation accept Kukkiwon ranks. Schools linked to the separate International Taekwon-Do Federation use their own certificates instead.

words.d: the taekwondo headquarters in Seoul, finished in 1972, that issues dan and poom certificates
a junior black-belt rank in taekwondo for students under fifteen
an official list that records who holds which rank or right

check.why: Poom ranks are junior black-belt ranks for students under fifteen.

check.q: Why does a registration number make a rank claim easier to test?
choices: It proves the teacher is the best fighter.
It means the rank is Olympic.

Another person can look it up in the issuing body's records.
check.why: A numbered certificate can be checked in the Kukkiwon's records by someone else.

lessons.title: What a Trademark Can Hold
lessons.mainIdea: A trademark protects a brand name for a business, but the general name of an art, such as judo or karate, cannot be owned.
reading: In the United States, the Lanham Act of 1946 is the main federal law on trademarks. A *trademark* is a word, name or symbol that tells buyers who offers a product or service. The United States Patent and Trademark Office keeps the federal register. A school can register its own name, logo or a special program title.

Trademark law will not let anyone own a *generic* word. A generic word is the common name for a whole kind of thing. "Karate," "judo" and "boxing" are generic names of arts. A company could register "Maple Street Karate," but not the word karate by itself. That rule keeps the name of a shared practice open to everyone.

Family names can become brands, and that can cause conflict. In Brazil, the Gracie family became well known for Brazilian jiu-jitsu, a grappling art that grew from judo taught there in the early 1900s. In the United States in the 1990s, members of the Gracie family went to court over who could use the family name on schools. The case shows that a lineage name can also be a business name.

words.d: a word, name or symbol that shows who offers a product or service
the common name for a whole kind of thing, which no one can own as a trademark
the 1946 United States law that governs federal trademarks

check.why: Relatives went to court over the Gracie name, showing a family lineage name can be a brand.

lessons.title: A Word the Olympic Movement Owns
lessons.mainIdea: A 1978 federal law gave the U.S. Olympic Committee control of the word Olympic, and the Supreme Court upheld that control in 1987.
reading: Congress passed the *Amateur Sports Act* in 1978. The law organized amateur sport in the United States under the U.S. Olympic Committee. It also gave the committee the right to control commercial use of the word "Olympic" and the five rings. In 1998, Congress renamed it the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act.

In the early 1980s, a San Francisco group planned an event called the "Gay Olympic Games." The U.S. Olympic Committee sued to stop the use of the word. In 1987, in San Francisco Arts and Athletics v. United States Olympic Committee, the Supreme Court ruled for the committee. The event went ahead in 1982 under the name Gay Games.

The case matters for martial arts because Olympic arts carry an extra name. Judo joined the Olympic program in 1964 and taekwondo became a medal sport in 2000. A school may teach Olympic-style judo, but using the word Olympic in a brand can raise legal questions. Here, ownership of a word comes from a statute, not from a lineage or a founder.

words.d: the 1978 U.S. law that organized amateur sport and gave the Olympic Committee control of the word Olympic
a written law passed by a legislature such as Congress
the highest court in the United States

look.title: What the Law Protects
look.text: The law gives the U.S. Olympic Committee the exclusive right to use the word Olympic and the five-ring symbol, and lets it sue anyone who uses them to sell goods or promote a competition without permission.
look.cite: Amateur Sports Act of 1978, 36 U.S.C. section 220506 (as amended in 1998)
look.prompt: Who holds the right to the word here? How is that different from a family or a federation holding a name?

check.q: What did the Amateur Sports Act of 1978 give the U.S. Olympic Committee?
choices: the right to run the Kodokan
control of commercial use of the word Olympic and the rings
the right to issue dan ranks
check.why: The 1978 law gave the committee control of commercial use of the word Olympic and the five rings.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in 1987 in San Francisco Arts and Athletics v. USOC?
choices: It ruled for the U.S. Olympic Committee.
It banned martial arts from the Olympics.

check.why: The Supreme Court ruled for the U.S. Olympic Committee in 1987.

check.q: Where does the Olympic committee's right to the word come from?
check.why: The right comes from a federal statute, the Amateur Sports Act.

lessons.title: Three Letters, Many Owners
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo has two major federations, and after its founder's death in 2002 the ITF split into several groups that each use the same name.
reading: Choi Hong-hi, a South Korean army general, founded the *International Taekwon-Do Federation* (ITF) in Seoul in 1966. He clashed with the South Korean government. In 1972 he moved to Canada and took the ITF's headquarters to Toronto. He later built ties with North Korea.

In 1973, a separate body, the World Taekwondo Federation, was founded in Seoul with South Korean government support. It led the path to the Olympics. Taekwondo was a demonstration sport in 1988 and 1992 and a full medal sport in 2000. In 2017 the federation shortened its name to *World Taekwondo*.

Choi died in Pyongyang, North Korea, in 2002. Soon after, the ITF divided into several rival groups. Each kept the name International Taekwon-Do Federation and each issues its own ranks. A student today may hold an "ITF" certificate from one group that another group does not accept. The name stayed the same while the owners multiplied.

words.d: the taekwondo body Choi Hong-hi founded in Seoul in 1966, later split into rival groups
the international federation founded in Seoul in 1973 that governs Olympic taekwondo
an organization that joins many schools or national groups under shared rules
competing with another group for the same thing

check.why: After Choi's death in 2002, the ITF divided into several groups that each kept the name.

check.q: In which year did taekwondo become a full Olympic medal sport?
check.why: Taekwondo was a demonstration sport in 1988 and 1992 and became a medal sport in 2000.

sections.title: A Nation Puts Its Name On

lessons.title: Naming Taekwondo
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo received its name in 1955 and became an official symbol of South Korea through federations, a national park and a 2018 law.
reading: After Japanese colonial rule ended in 1945, several schools called *kwan* opened in Seoul. Each kwan used its own name for its art. In 1955, Korean teachers and officials agreed on a single name: taekwondo. Choi Hong-hi is widely credited with proposing it. The name joins three Korean words, often translated as foot, fist and way.

The Korea Taekwondo Association, founded in 1959, worked to bring the kwan under one national body. Unifying the schools took years. The government saw a shared national art as useful for military training, for schools and for showing Korea to the world. Taekwondo demonstration teams toured abroad in the 1960s and 1970s.

The state's role grew over time. A national taekwondo park called Taekwondowon opened in 2014 in Muju County. In 2018, South Korea's National Assembly passed a law naming taekwondo the country's *national sport*. A name that began as a choice among teachers became a legal symbol of a nation.

words.d: a Korean word for a hall or school; used for the first taekwondo schools after 1945
a sport a country names by law or custom as a symbol of itself
the image a country presents to the world through symbols it chooses, such as a sport

look.title: Many Signs, One Word

check.why: The name taekwondo was agreed on in 1955.

check.why: In 2018 the National Assembly passed a law naming taekwondo the national sport.

check.q: What was a kwan in the years after 1945?
choices: a Korean school or hall for the art
check.why: Kwan were the first schools that opened in Seoul after 1945.

lessons.title: Muay Thai and the Thai State
lessons.mainIdea: Thailand links Muay Thai to national history through an honored legend, state-backed stadiums and a federation that won full IOC recognition in 2021.
reading: Thai tradition tells of Nai Khanom Tom, a fighter captured by Burmese forces after the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767. In the story, he wins his freedom by defeating many opponents before a Burmese king. The account comes from later chronicles and is best read as a *legend*. Thailand marks March 17 as National Muay Thai Day in his honor.

In the twentieth century, Bangkok's two great stadiums became national stages. Rajadamnern Stadium opened in 1945. Lumpinee Stadium opened in 1956 and was run by the Royal Thai Army. Fight nights at these stadiums were broadcast across the country. The name "Muay Thai," meaning Thai boxing, tied the sport to the nation itself.

The International Federation of Muaythai Associations (IFMA) was founded in 1993 to organize amateur Muay Thai worldwide. The International Olympic Committee gave IFMA provisional *recognition* in 2016 and full recognition in 2021. Recognition does not put a sport on the Olympic program. It does mean the IOC accepts IFMA as the sport's world governing body.

words.d: a traditional story about the past that cannot be fully checked in records
the IOC's formal acceptance of a group as a sport's world governing body
the International Federation of Muaythai Associations, founded in 1993

look.prompt: How many years passed between provisional and full IOC recognition?

check.q: How should a historian treat the story of Nai Khanom Tom?
choices: as a legend from later chronicles
check.why: The Nai Khanom Tom account comes from later chronicles and is best read as a legend.

check.q: Which Bangkok stadium was run by the Royal Thai Army?
check.why: Lumpinee Stadium, opened in 1956, was run by the Royal Thai Army.

check.q: What did IOC recognition of IFMA in 2021 mean?
choices: The IOC accepts IFMA as Muay Thai's world governing body.
Muay Thai joined the 2024 Olympic program.
check.why: Recognition means the IOC accepts IFMA as the governing body; it does not add the sport to the Games.

lessons.title: Heritage Lists and Shared Names
lessons.mainIdea: UNESCO's heritage lists let nations name martial practices as their living heritage, and sometimes two nations claim related arts.
reading: In 2003, UNESCO adopted the Convention for the Safeguarding of the *Intangible Cultural Heritage*. Intangible heritage means living practices, such as songs, festivals and crafts, rather than buildings. Countries nominate practices for UNESCO's lists. A place on the list is a statement by a nation about what belongs to its people.

Several martial practices are on the list. Iran's pahlevani and zoorkhaneh rituals and Turkey's Kırkpınar oil wrestling festival were added in 2010. Korea's taekkyeon was added in 2011. Brazil's capoeira circle, the roda, was added in 2014. Brazil had already named capoeira national heritage in 2008.

Sometimes a listing shows how names cross borders. In 2018, North Korea and South Korea were jointly inscribed for ssireum, a form of Korean wrestling, the first joint listing by the two states. In 2019, Indonesia's pencak silat and Malaysia's silat were inscribed as two separate entries. Each nation named its own tradition within a family of related arts.

words.d: living practices, such as festivals, songs and crafts, that a community passes on
the United Nations agency for education, science and culture
to add a practice officially to a UNESCO list

lessons.title: Diaspora Rooms
lessons.mainIdea: Migrants carried martial arts to new countries, and diaspora schools kept, changed and renamed those arts far from where they began.
reading: A *diaspora* is a community that lives far from its homeland but keeps ties to it. Japanese immigrants began arriving in Hawaii in large numbers in the 1880s to work on sugar plantations. They built temples, language schools and judo clubs. In 1934, the Okinawan karate teacher Miyagi Chōjun visited Hawaii to teach in the islands' Okinawan community.

Filipino workers came to Hawaii and California in the 1920s and 1930s. Many of them practiced arnis, also called eskrima, a Filipino art. For decades it was taught quietly among friends and family. In 1966, Angel Cabales opened a school in Stockton, California, that is often called the first public eskrima school in the United States.

Brazilian teachers brought capoeira to New York and other U.S. cities in the 1970s. A diaspora school often faces two sets of questions. Elders at home may ask whether it keeps the tradition. New students may ask whether it welcomes them. A school's name, its teacher's lineage and its ties to the homeland all become part of its answer.

words.d: a community living far from its homeland that keeps ties to it
a Filipino martial art, also called eskrima or kali
people moving from one country or region to live in another

lessons.title: Evidence, Not a Feeling
lessons.mainIdea: Strong claims about a name rest on dated records, such as the 1936 Naha meeting that chose the written name for karate.
reading: The word karate was once written with characters meaning "Chinese hand." On October 25, 1936, leading Okinawan teachers met in Naha at a meeting hosted by a local newspaper. They agreed to use characters meaning "empty hand" instead. The newspaper printed a report of the meeting. In 2005, the Okinawa Prefectural Assembly named October 25 as Karate Day.

That meeting is strong *evidence* because it has a date, a place, named people and a printed record. Other claims about karate's past rest on family memory. *Oral history*, the memories people tell and record, is valuable, and historians collect it carefully. They also compare it with letters, photographs, newspapers and official registers.

Historians ask the same questions of any claim to a name. Who made the record, and when? Did anyone gain from it? Does a second, independent source agree? A certificate, a trademark, a heritage listing and a legend can all be true in their own way. Each answers a different question about who holds a name.

words.d: records or objects that support a claim about the past
memories that people tell aloud, which historians record and study
a record made by someone separate from the person making a claim
